# On the Strange Comfort of Not Knowing

There's a peculiar peace that settles over you when you finally accept that you don't have to understand everything. I've been thinking about this a lot lately—how we're culturally conditioned to treat uncertainty like a disease, something to be cured with enough research, enough time, enough thinking. But what if uncertainty is actually the default state of existence, and our constant striving for answers is the real aberration?

I noticed this feeling most acutely the other day while watching rain. Not contemplating it, not photographing it for social media, just watching it fall on leaves that couldn't possibly care about my philosophical musings. The rain was doing its thing, the leaves were receiving it, and somewhere in that interaction was a completeness that required no interpretation. I didn't need to understand cloud formation or plant physiology to appreciate what I was seeing. The mystery didn't diminish the experience—it deepened it.

We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet somehow anxiety levels have never been higher. I wonder if there's a connection. When you can Google any question instantly, the expectation becomes that you *should* know the answer. The space between question and answer has collapsed. There's no time for wondering anymore, no room for the productive sitting-with-not-knowing that characterized human experience for most of our history.

My grandmother, who passed away five years ago, used to say "I'll never know" about things with a kind of contentment that baffled younger me. Why wouldn't you try to find out? Now I understand she wasn't being lazy or incurious. She was making a deliberate choice about which mysteries to pursue and which to let breathe. Not every question deserves a definitive answer. Some are better left as questions.

This is especially true about other people. We spend so much energy trying to figure out why people do what they do, what they *really* mean, whether they like us, what they think about us. We construct elaborate theories based on minimal evidence, then build entire emotional structures on these theories. The exhaustion of it all. And for what? You could spend your entire life trying to understand another person and still never fully succeed. They're not a puzzle with a solution. They're a person, irreducibly complex, constantly changing, fundamentally private in ways you'll never quite access.

I think about this with relationships that ended. There's usually this period where you endlessly analyze: What did I do wrong? What do they really think of me now? Could we have salvaged it? The mind churns and churns, producing no useful output. Eventually, most people give up on finding the "correct" interpretation of events. You just... move on. Not because you found the answer, but because you stopped needing to.

There's also something deeply humanizing about admitting ignorance. I notice that people I respect most—truly wise people, not just educated ones—seem comfortable saying "I don't know" more often than others. There's no defensive posturing, no rush to fill silence with speculation presented as fact. They sit with not knowing and somehow seem more present for it.

I've been thinking about love this way too. The more you try to define it, dissect it, understand exactly why you love someone, the more it slips away. The good relationships I've observed aren't the ones where people have everything figured out. They're the ones where people are willing to just... show up. To be bewildered together. To make it work not because they understand each other perfectly, but despite understanding each other only partially.

There's a religious quality to this acceptance, I think, though you don't need to be religious to access it. It's the surrender that mystics speak of. Not surrender as defeat, but as a kind of intelligent yielding. A recognition that some forces are larger than your understanding of them.

The older I get, the more comfortable I become with my own inconsistency. I hold beliefs that contradict each other. I do things my values don't endorse. I feel ways I can't justify. Once this troubled me endlessly. Why can't I be coherent? Why can't I resolve these contradictions? Now I see that contradiction might not be a bug but a feature. Maybe humans aren't supposed to be perfectly consistent. Maybe we're supposed to be paradoxical, holding multiple truths simultaneously, trying on different ways of being.

I think about death sometimes, and how the ultimate mystery is waiting for everyone. No amount of understanding will change that final unknowing. But somehow, accepting this feels lighter than fighting it. The pretense that we can know everything, control everything, predict everything—that's heavy. You're always one step behind, always catching up to reality as it moves past you.

There's a freedom in this realization, though. If you're never going to fully understand anyway, you might as well stop trying so hard. Might as well look around more. Listen better. Pay attention to the particular texture of your immediate experience rather than constantly analyzing it.

This isn't an argument for abandonment of reason or curiosity. I still read, still think, still try to learn. But I'm more selective now about where I direct that effort. I'm less interested in understanding people and more interested in simply knowing them. Less interested in explaining emotions and more interested in feeling them. Less interested in the right answer and more interested in the right question.

Sometimes I think the most sophisticated thing a human can do is be genuinely uncertain and genuinely okay with it. To hold the question and not frantically search for an exit. To say "I don't know, and maybe that's alright" and really mean it.

The rain is falling again as I write this, and I'm not trying to understand it. I'm just listening to what it sounds like against the window, and that seems like enough.
